name: SHISHITO CORLEONE BURGER (comes with Shishito Peppers)

recipe.history:
Shishito peppers — Capsicum annuum — are a thin-skinned, finger-length Japanese variety whose name derives from the Japanese word for lion, shishi, owing to the wrinkled, lion-faced appearance of the tip of the pepper. They are believed to have originated in the Iberian Peninsula and arrived in Japan via Portuguese traders in the sixteenth century, where Japanese horticulturists selectively bred out most of the heat to produce the mild, sweet, slightly smoky variety known today. In Japan they are most classically prepared as agemono — deep fried or blistered in a dry pan or on a grill until charred and collapsing, then seasoned with nothing more than flaky salt or a dipping sauce of ponzu. The famous culinary quirk of the shishito is that approximately one in ten peppers in any given batch carries a surprising jolt of heat, a genetic remnant of the pepper's spicier ancestors, making eating them a gentle game of Russian roulette that has delighted diners for centuries across East Asia.

Shishito peppers arrived in American restaurant culture in the early 2000s, riding the wave of Japanese culinary influence that also brought izakaya-style eating and the small-plates format to urban dining. David Chang and other chefs influenced by Japanese bar food culture helped bring blistered shishitos — charred in a ripping hot pan, finished with flaky sea salt and sometimes a squeeze of lemon — onto menus as a bar snack and appetizer that was simultaneously elegant and brutally simple. Their migration to the burger was inevitable: a pepper that blisters beautifully, holds its shape under heat, and delivers a complex roasted flavor with occasional surprise heat is exactly the kind of topping that makes a burger memorable. Laid across a beef patty they add color, texture, a subtle sweetness from the char, and that inimitable quality of a great izakaya snack transported to an American classic.

I have a distinct memory of the first shishito I ever bit into that was actually spicy. I was at a bar in the East Village, eating a bowl of blistered shishitos with a beer, feeling relaxed and slightly smug about how mild they were, and then one of them — ordinary looking, no warning — detonated quietly in my mouth with a clean, bright heat that made me blink and laugh out loud at the same time. The person across from me gave me a knowing look. That is what shishitos do: they remind you that even the mildest, most familiar ingredients carry the capacity to surprise. I started putting them on burgers shortly after that night, blistering them until they were fully collapsed and charred at the edges, and the first time I laid a small pile of them across a medium-rare patty I knew it was one of those combinations that felt inevitable in hindsight.

Cooking a burger to medium rare — 130 to 135 degrees Fahrenheit, 54 to 57 degrees Celsius — is the foundational act of showing respect to every ingredient in the assembly. Shishito peppers, with their delicate sweetness and occasional heat, require a partner that can hold its own in terms of flavor and moisture. An overcooked patty — grey and dry at 160 degrees — would make the blistered peppers feel out of place, their brightness orphaned atop something that has given up. A medium-rare patty is warm and pink and running with savory juices, a living counterpart to the charred, slightly smoky pepper. They meet in the middle: fire and juice, char and fat, the Corleone authority of a perfectly cooked burger making an offer the shishito cannot refuse. Medium rare is the only temperature at which all of this makes sense.
ingredients: 1 egg + 1 tbsp water for egg wash
680g ground beef (80/20 chuck blend), freshly ground
1/2 white onion, thinly sliced into rings
instructions: 1. Make the buns: Combine warm milk, sugar, and yeast in the bowl of a stand mixer. Let sit 5 minutes until foamy.
2. Add egg and softened butter. Mix briefly. Add bread flour and salt. Knead with dough hook on medium speed for 8 minutes until smooth and slightly tacky.
3. Transfer to an oiled bowl, cover with plastic wrap, and let rise 1 to 1.5 hours until doubled.
4. Divide into 4 portions (~150g each), shape into tight rounds, place on a parchment-lined baking sheet, cover, and proof 45 minutes.
5. Preheat oven to 375°F (190°C). Brush with egg wash and sprinkle with sesame seeds. Bake 16 to 18 minutes until deep golden. Cool on a rack.
6. Make the miso mayo: Whisk together mayonnaise, white miso paste, rice wine vinegar, honey, and sesame oil until smooth and fully combined. Refrigerate until needed.

7. Blister the shishito peppers: Heat a dry cast iron skillet or heavy pan over high heat until very hot and beginning to smoke. Add olive oil and shishito peppers in a single layer. Do not crowd the pan — work in batches if needed. Cook undisturbed for 2 minutes until deeply charred on the bottom. Toss and cook another 2 minutes until blistered and collapsed all over. Transfer to a bowl. Toss immediately with lemon juice, soy sauce, and flaky sea salt. Set aside.

8. Prepare the patties: Divide ground beef into 4 equal portions (170g each). Form into 3/4-inch thick patties with a center dimple. Season both sides generously with salt, pepper, and smoked paprika immediately before cooking.
9. Heat a cast iron skillet over high heat until smoking. Add a thin film of neutral oil.
10. Place patties in the pan. Cook 2 minutes undisturbed to develop a crust. Flip once. Top each patty with a slice of aged white cheddar immediately.
11. Cook 1.5 to 2 minutes more, tenting loosely with foil, until an instant-read thermometer reads 130 to 135°F (54 to 57°C) for medium rare. Transfer to a wire rack and rest 3 minutes.
12. Toast the buns: Butter cut sides and toast face-down in a skillet over medium heat until golden, about 1 minute.
13. Assemble: Spread miso mayo generously on both cut faces of each bun.
14. Layer shredded lettuce on the bottom bun, then tomato slices and white onion rings.
15. Set the medium-rare cheddar-topped patty on the vegetables. Arrange 5 to 6 blistered shishito peppers on top of the patty, leaving stems on for presentation.
16. Cap with the top bun and serve immediately. Warn your guests about the hot one.
